Sensitivity, Specificity, and Accuracy of Diagnostic Studies: Across eight studies involving 3,449 participants, the pooled sensitivity was 42% (95% credible interval [CrI]: 31–55%), and the specificity was 91% (95% CrI: 85–95%). Seven studies with 3,365 participants showed a sensitivity of 35% (95% CrI: 22–50%) and specificity of 95% (95% CrI: 89–98%). In inpatient settings, six studies with 2,253 participants demonstrated a sensitivity of 52% (95% CrI: 40–64%) and specificity of 87% (95% CrI: 78–93%). For outpatients, four studies with 1,196 participants showed a sensitivity of 29% (95% CrI: 17–47%) and specificity of 96% (95% CrI: 91–99%). 2. Diagnostic Performance by CD4 Cell Count: For individuals with CD4 counts >200, three studies (738 participants) reported a sensitivity of 16% (95% CrI: 8–31%) and specificity of 94% (95% CrI: 81–97%). For CD4 ≤200, four studies (1,825 participants) showed a sensitivity of 45% (95% CrI: 31–61%) and specificity of 89% (95% CrI: 77–94%). For CD4 ≤100, four studies (1,239 participants) reported a sensitivity of 54% (95% CrI: 38–69%) and specificity of 88% (95% CrI: 77–94%). 3. WHO Recommendations for Tuberculosis (TB) Treatment in People Living with HIV: TB patients living with HIV should receive the same duration of daily TB treatment as HIV-negative TB patients (strong recommendation, high certainty of evidence). This includes at least six months of treatment, with some expert groups recommending extended treatment in specific cases to reduce relapse rates. For individuals with TB and histoplasmosis co-infection, TB therapy should follow WHO guidelines, balancing the risks of drug resistance and drug-drug interactions (e.g., rifampicin reducing itraconazole levels). 4. Integrated Care for HIV-Associated TB: Early initiation of TB treatment and antiretroviral therapy (ART) is critical for reducing mortality and improving outcomes. WHO recommends integrated care delivery for TB and HIV, with ART provided in TB treatment settings to improve uptake and timeliness. 5. TB Preventive Treatment (TPT) for People Living with HIV: Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes individuals on ART, pregnant women, and those previously treated for TB, regardless of immune suppression or latent TB infection (LTBI) testing availability. Recommended TPT regimens include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or four months of daily rifampicin. In high TB transmission settings, 36 months of daily isoniazid is conditionally recommended. 6. Screening and Testing for TB Infection: WHO recommends symptom-based screening (current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats) to rule out active TB before initiating TPT. Chest radiography may be used as an additional tool but should not delay TPT initiation. Testing for TB infection can be done using tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA). Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) are also recommended, with evidence suggesting similar diagnostic accuracy to IGRAs and greater accuracy than TSTs. 7. Special Considerations for Pregnant Women: Pregnant women living with HIV are at increased risk of TB, which can have severe consequences for both mother and fetus. Preventive treatment with isoniazid or rifampicin is considered safe during pregnancy and should not be withheld. 8. Duration of TB Treatment: Evidence supports the use of daily isoniazid for up to nine months to maximize benefit. Shorter regimens, such as three months of daily rifampicin plus isoniazid or one month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, are also effective and may improve adherence. 9. Long-Term Preventive Therapy: Continuous isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) for 36 months or longer has been shown to reduce TB risk by 38% compared to six months of IPT in high TB burden settings. 10. Challenges and Recommendations: Clinicians should consider local contexts, drug interactions, and resistance profiles when managing co-infections. These findings and recommendations emphasize the importance of tailored, evidence-based approaches to TB prevention and treatment in people living with HIV, with a focus on integrated care and addressing specific population needs.
